title: Running Workflows in Containers knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Running Workflows in Containers?
options: A job-level container standardizes the job environment, but it still depends on runner capabilities, container networking, image availability, and mounted workspace behavior.
Give every job write permission to avoid troubleshooting authorization errors.
Print all environment variables and event payloads to make the run easier to debug.
Run untrusted pull-request code in the same job that holds production credentials.
questions.answer_key: A job-level container standardizes the job environment, but it still depends on runner capabilities, container networking, image availability, and mounted workspace behavior.
questions.explanation: This is the central behavior of running workflows in containers: A job-level container standardizes the job environment, but it still depends on runner capabilities, container networking, image availability, and mounted workspace behavior. Validate configuration and behavior against the current official reference before production use.

questions.prompt: A team is working with “Job-level container”. Which practice best fits this topic?
options: Print all environment variables and event payloads to make the run easier to debug.
Run untrusted pull-request code in the same job that holds production credentials.
Build and identify an image deterministically, grant only required registry permissions, scan/verify before promotion, and prefer immutable digests or traceable tags over mutable “latest” references.
Give every job write permission to avoid troubleshooting authorization errors.
questions.answer_key: Build and identify an image deterministically, grant only required registry permissions, scan/verify before promotion, and prefer immutable digests or traceable tags over mutable “latest” references.
questions.explanation: Job-level container: Build and identify an image deterministically, grant only required registry permissions, scan/verify before promotion, and prefer immutable digests or traceable tags over mutable “latest” references. questions.prompt: How should a reviewer verify a change related to running workflows in containers?
options: Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
Assume the workflow is correct as soon as the YAML file is committed.
Retry every failure without looking at the exit code or preserving evidence.
Publish the workflow to production before reviewing its triggers and permissions.
questions.answer_key: Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Reliable verification uses observable evidence. For this lesson, consider: A job-level container standardizes the job environment, but it still depends on runner capabilities, container networking, image availability, and mounted workspace behavior. A syntax check alone cannot prove remote execution, permissions, or deployment behavior.
